stories.headline: MIT researchers say GPT-6 Astra can read and edit neural network weights directly
stories.why_read: The biggest thing on Hacker News today: a frontier model fixing a smaller model by reasoning about its raw weights, with no gradient descent involved.
body: In 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming,' Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab of MIT CSAIL report that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at reading and writing network weights. Given the 17,253 raw weights of a small policy network and no tools, GPT-6 Astra named the game it was trained on (Breakout, 99% confident). It also wrote small game-playing networks from scratch that beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

The headline result is on a real language model. Asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without training, Astra found a weight-level cause of the reasoning loops Qwen's own model card warns about, then edited 0.016% of the weights. MATH-500 went from 7.9% to 48.1% at the same sampling settings, and IFEval roughly tripled. The authors call these early results, but if they hold up, optimizers like Adam start to look like one option among several. Interpretability gets a new tool too.

stories.headline: TSMC is reportedly in site talks with Sherman, Texas, for a fab complex of up to $120 billion
stories.why_read: If it happens, a leading-edge fab cluster would sit north of Dallas, with thousands of jobs and a large new power load on the Texas grid.
body: Citing local outlets including the Dallas Business Journal, @jukan05 reports that Sherman, in Grayson County north of Dallas, has entered site-selection talks with TSMC. The plan described starts with about $45 billion for two fabs and could grow to six fabs and $120 billion over the medium to long term.

The reported timeline has about 5,000 hires over six years and volume production starting in late 2029. These are site-selection talks, not an announcement, so treat the numbers as a proposal. Together with Samsung in Taylor and Texas Instruments already in Sherman, it would make North and Central Texas a serious semiconductor corridor.

stories.headline: Debian patched a CVSS 9.8 Linux TCP bug on October 16. Ubuntu still hasn't
stories.why_read: If your fleet runs Ubuntu LTS, check today. A root exploit for this bug is out, and Canonical hasn't shipped fixed kernels.
body: CVE-2026-98432 is a critical bug in the Linux kernel's TCP code. According to a widely shared post on chalmovsky.com, it dates back to 2016, can be triggered remotely, and Anthropic says it built a working root exploit for it. Debian shipped a fix on October 16. As of November 2 at 14:48 UTC, the author says Ubuntu still listed every supported release, LTS included, as 'Vulnerable.' Volunteer-run distros like Arch and Alpine have also patched.

A separate freenode write-up confirms that no fixed kernels exist yet for 22.04, 24.04 or 26.04 and that Canonical hasn't given an ETA. The author took their Ubuntu servers offline and is migrating them off. Whatever you decide about Ubuntu long term, the practical step is the same: list your exposed Ubuntu hosts, and consider a patched mainline kernel, a mitigation, or moving the workload until packages arrive. The post got more than 1,500 points on HN.

stories.headline: Revolut moved 2,000 engineers from Claude and Codex to self-hosted GLM
stories.why_read: A concrete enterprise case for open weights: about a tenth of the cost, and the company says its engineers got faster, not slower.
body: X's news summary of the story says Revolut switched its roughly 2,000 engineers from paid APIs like Claude and Codex to GLM, an open-weight model it self-hosts on 56 Nvidia GPUs. The change happened in April. Costs fell to about 30 cents per million tokens, roughly a tenth of what Revolut paid before, and the company reports a 60% boost in coding productivity and 70% shorter lead times.

Frontier models are now kept for the exceptions, and engineers use the in-house model for routine work like Jira updates. The productivity figures are self-reported, and HN commenters are arguing about them. Still, for anyone pricing agents for an IT org, this is the clearest public 'own the inference' playbook yet.

stories.headline: Training on 'compute islands' and a Gemma haiku from orbit: the case for space data centers gets real
stories.why_read: Musk says superintelligence compute will 'round up to 100%' in space. This week also brought the first evidence that the engineering can work.
body: X's news summary pulls together two threads. Rohan Anil describes algorithms that keep training a model across 'compute islands,' clusters with patchy links between them, and demonstrated a run across sites 9,000 miles apart. Separately, Google's Project Suncatcher launched a prototype satellite on October 1, and on October 30 it produced the first AI output from orbit: a haiku from a Gemma 4 model.

Elon Musk, in a post Anand bookmarked, went much further: future superintelligence compute will be 'overwhelmingly in space,' and by overwhelmingly he means it 'will round up to 100%.' A haiku is a long way from a gigawatt cluster. But training that tolerates flaky links is exactly what a Starlink-style compute constellation would need.

stories.headline: Verification loops beat adversarial reviews: two engineers on what agent-era coding work is now
stories.why_read: Two posts Anand reposted make the same point from different directions: put your tokens and your effort into proving that code works.
body: Cindy Sridharan argues that designing good verification loops is now 'most of the job.' She just landed a refactor she started in January, and she says it was good she waited because the January version was 'buggy af.' Her post walks through the verification process she uses for refactors and notes that she uses different ones for performance work.

Lauren (@poteto) offers a hot take that has passed 6,000 likes: adversarial code reviews by agents are 'mostly a waste of tokens.' She says agents tend to get lost in nitpicks and YAGNIs, so she has updated her pstack setup to use its interrogate skill less and now prefers empirical checks combined with formal verification. If you're building review bots, it's a useful counterweight.

stories.headline: SLAC finds direct proof of altermagnetism, a third kind of magnetism
stories.why_read: For about 90 years, physics recognized two kinds of magnetic order in materials. Now there's solid evidence for a third, with possible uses in memory and data centers.
body: Ferromagnets line all their spins up. Antiferromagnets, discovered in 1933, alternate spins so they cancel out. In 2022, theorists proposed 'altermagnets,' which have the zero net magnetization of an antiferromagnet but can still carry the spin currents of a ferromagnet. In a paper in Science, a team led by SLAC's Daniel Jost reports direct experimental evidence of chirality, a screw-like asymmetry, in the spins of manganese telluride (MnTe).

The team says that signal is impossible to explain without altermagnetism, which makes this the strongest confirmation yet. Why it matters beyond the lab: a magnet with no stray field that can still steer spin currents is the kind of material you'd want for denser, faster memory and spintronics. SLAC names quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers as possible uses.

stories.headline: Washington Post: the prospect of SpaceX running its own mobile network has rattled the big carriers
stories.why_read: Starlink's direct-to-cell service could grow from a backup feature for carriers into a competitor. Telecom insiders are taking that seriously.
body: In an exclusive Anand reposted, the Washington Post reports that the possibility of SpaceX securing an agreement to operate a mobile network has worried major carriers. The Post based this on interviews with nearly a dozen people in the telecom industry, who fear Elon Musk could threaten their business.

So far, Starlink's direct-to-cell service has been something carriers partner with to fill dead zones. Running a network itself would put SpaceX on the other side of the table, with spectrum, satellites and an existing customer base. The post is light on terms, so watch for which spectrum and which partner come up next.

stories.headline: Tesla's Texas Megapack factory gets Foreign-Trade Zone approval
stories.why_read: A quiet Federal Register notice that could help Megapack costs for a factory that depends on imported components.
body: Sawyer Merritt points to a Federal Register notice: the Foreign-Trade Zones Board has authorized Tesla's proposed production activity at its Texas Megapack factory on a limited basis for 14 months.

In a foreign-trade zone, a manufacturer can work with imported components before they formally enter the U.S. customs market. It defers duties until finished products enter the country, and anything exported directly from the zone skips U.S. duties entirely. For a product built around imported cells, that's real money, and with AI data centers buying grid batteries, it lands at a good time.

stories.headline: Video: FSD sees a crash happening behind the car and moves out of the way
stories.why_read: A short clip that shows the 360-degree awareness a human driver checking the rearview mirror can't match.
body: @WaitWhat shared a clip in which a Tesla on FSD reacts to an accident unfolding behind it and pulls out of the way. 'It's always watching all around the car,' the post says.

It's one video, not data. But it's a clean example of the kind of event robotaxi skeptics say is hard: reacting to something outside the driver's line of sight, in time for it to matter. Anand reposted it along with a Montreal influencer's Tesla review.

stories.headline: The bull case for merging Tesla and SpaceX, in two lists
stories.why_read: A clear way to frame a debate that keeps coming up: SpaceX needs seven things from Tesla, and Tesla needs one thing from SpaceX.
body: @CuriousPejjy lists what SpaceX needs from Tesla: Optimus robots, Megapacks, solar, batteries, real-world AI data, autonomous cars and chip design. Tesla, in this framing, mainly needs one thing from SpaceX: lots of AI compute. Renting that compute would eat into Tesla's profits.

The conclusion is to merge sooner rather than later, before the two valuations drift further apart, and to own more of the combined company. It's an investor's argument, not reporting, but it pairs well with today's SpaceX compute-in-orbit and mobile-network stories.

stories.headline: Nvidia open-sources Auto Ontology, a semantic layer that grounds agents in what your data means
stories.why_read: For anyone wiring agents to enterprise data: this targets the 'right SQL, wrong metric' problem, and it speaks MCP.
body: Nvidia's pitch: agents can already query databases, but 'a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong.' Auto Ontology builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. It reconciles metric definitions across systems, checks generated queries against certified definitions and lineage, and returns provenance with every answer. It serves that context to any agent harness through MCP, a CLI and an API.

The stack is a Next.js front end, a FastAPI and LangChain backend, and Postgres with pgvector, with inference through NVIDIA NIM. It deploys with Helm on Kubernetes or with Docker Compose. It's Apache-2.0 and had about 1.7k stars at fetch time, though Nvidia isn't accepting outside contributions yet.

stories.headline: DeepSeek's open super-agent prototype cut its slowest completion times nearly in half
stories.why_read: An MIT-licensed reference design for multi-agent setups: a router, isolated workers and a watchdog. It's very close to how a bot fleet works.
body: According to X's news summary, DeepSeek's dsh-superagent runs on DeepSeek Harness with two layers. A Router filters incoming conversations and hands work to isolated Worker sessions, while a Watchdog monitors progress. In tests with noisy input streams and 20 requests, the slowest completion times dropped from 29.5 to 15.7 minutes compared with a single-session setup.

It's released as research code under the MIT license, and the summary flags unsolved security issues such as credential handling. Still, if you run several specialized bots, the router-plus-watchdog pattern is worth studying.

stories.headline: Meituan's LongCat-2.5: 1.6 trillion parameters, 48 billion active, built for long agent tasks
stories.why_read: Another very large Chinese model at aggressive prices. The Terminal Bench number is the one to verify.
body: X's news summary says LongCat-2.5 has 1.6 trillion total parameters with 48 billion active per token, and it processes images and text through a shared token backbone. It's available through the API at longcat.ai, with 10 million free tokens for new users and about $0.30 per million uncached input tokens.

Meituan's own benchmarks claim 88.4 on Terminal Bench and 55.4 on 3DCodeBench, which would put it near the top models. Independent verification is still pending. Developers are pointing to its focus on long-horizon agent work and its optimizations for Chinese hardware.

stories.headline: Hydrogen-1.0: a 753B open-weight model trained on real lab records for scientific discovery
stories.why_read: A different approach to open models: instead of more web text, it's fine-tuned on full experiment cycles, from design to outcome.
body: Hangzhou-based Deep Principle released Hydrogen-1.0 on November 2, according to X's news summary. It's a 753-billion-parameter model built from Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and fine-tuned on complete lab records: experiment designs, procedures, observations and outcomes.

The company reports 38.3% on FrontierScience-Research multi-step problems and 93.0% on GPQA-Diamond, often edging out GPT-6 Astra. Those are vendor numbers. It's on Hugging Face under an MIT license, with lab-simulation interfaces, so researchers can check the claims themselves.

stories.headline: Gemini 4 Carbon edges Claude Opus 5.5 for the top spot on the Artificial Analysis index
stories.why_read: The frontier is now separated by single points: 59, 58, 57 and 55. Price and reliability matter more than rank.
body: X's news summary reports Gemini 4 Carbon at 59 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 at 58, GPT-6 Astra at 57 and GPT-6.1 Sol at 55. It does especially well on cybersecurity, long-context reasoning and math.

Google launched it in late October and is rolling it out first to select cyber defenders through its Fairwind Program before wider access. With the top four this close, the practical question for your coding and bot defaults is cost and consistency, not leaderboard position.

stories.headline: Altman says OpenAI's next GPT is coming 'very soon,' and a 'Le GPT Fat' tease points at GPT-6.2 Astra
stories.why_read: Two signals from the same 24 hours suggest the next OpenAI release is close. Plan your evals.
body: Speaking at ADIPEC in Abu Dhabi on November 2, Sam Altman said OpenAI's next model, which he described as able to coordinate agents without a hierarchy, will release very soon. The announcement followed work on the Navier-Stokes challenge, and he called it one of AI's most incredible moments. It came alongside deals with ADNOC, G42, Mubadala and Inception42, according to X's news summary.

Separately, an OpenAI insider's playful 'Le GPT Fat' post set off speculation about GPT-6.2 Astra, a larger, more compute-hungry internal model that Codex analytics reportedly show by name. OpenAI hasn't confirmed it, so treat the size rumors as rumors.

stories.headline: Grok Bot can now post on X, and SpaceXSI's internal Data Bot shows what that looks like at work
stories.why_read: Directly relevant to your fleet: a new posting capability, plus a real-world account of a Grok Bot doing 70 hours of data work in a week.
body: Alex Michael, in a post Anand reposted, announced that Grok Bot can now post on X on your behalf. For a bot fleet, that means approval rules for posting matter even more.

X's news summary describes SpaceXSI's Data Bot, powered by Grok Bot, which gives every employee data-science help over DMs or Slack: metrics tracking, experiment analysis and quick queries. Data scientist Sally Xu says it handled 70 hours of routine work in one week, freeing the data team for strategic projects. People still handle the complex work.

stories.headline: Coinbase opens a sign-up page for AI agents to trade through MCP
stories.why_read: Agents with trading permissions are now a product. The boundaries you set are the whole story.
body: Coinbase launched a page on November 2 that lets agents like Grok and Claude connect to user accounts through the Model Context Protocol, according to X's news summary. Agents can review portfolios, check markets and execute trades in crypto, stocks and derivatives, within limits the user sets.

A global agent trading competition with up to $2 million in prizes starts November 4. Supporters see a lead in agent-driven finance. Critics want clearer transparency and liability rules. Anyone thinking about money-moving agents should read both sides.

stories.headline: Claude and Grok API outputs get invisible watermarks to meet the EU AI Act
stories.why_read: Starting this week, text from major models will carry statistical marks, so expect questions about AI-written work reports.
body: Per X's news summary, Anthropic begins watermarking outputs from Claude models including Mythos 5 and Opus 4.7 on November 3. The marks are subtle statistical patterns in word choice that survive copying and light edits without changing meaning. SpaceXSI turns watermarking on by default for Grok API outputs from November 7 across seven models.

Both are responses to the EU AI Act's requirement that synthetic content be detectable. Commenters are asking whether paraphrasing or local models can strip the marks. Open-weight models you host yourself aren't covered by these vendor changes.

stories.headline: Resisting cognitive surrender: how to keep thinking while agents write the code
stories.why_read: An honest essay about the pull to accept whatever the agent says, and practical ways to stay in the loop.
body: Kunal (knlb.dev) defines cognitive surrender as uncritically accepting agent output without exploring alternatives. It's fast, it isn't tiring, and it's seductive. He describes peer pressure, agents' RLHF-trained confidence, and a kind of Gell-Mann amnesia: when you know the domain, you see how much the output can be simplified, and when you don't, the agents seem brilliant.

His fixes include choosing a 'vibe limit,' watching for automation bias, forcing yourself into the loop, insisting on comprehensible output, and delegating deliberately. X's news summary shows Addy Osmani making the same argument today, citing Anthropic's finding that oversight requires sharp coding judgment.

stories.headline: Cloudflare halved its DNS propagation delay and cut peak memory 85%
stories.why_read: A careful systems write-up on doing the smallest safe amount of work, and on proving it's safe.
body: Alex Fattouche explains that Cloudflare's Zone Builder now handles about 700 DNS record changes per second, up from 250 in 2022, plus about 100 other events. Some zones hold more than 20 million records. Record changes were already built incrementally, but zone-setting changes, such as Universal SSL changing CAA records at the zone apex, still triggered full rebuilds of very large zones.

The fix was a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build it can prove is safe, plus a scheduler that batches work for the same zone. Peak memory fell 85%, and the extra headroom let them shorten resilience waits, halving the time from a DNS change to its write into Quicksilver.

stories.headline: Egoless mathematics in the AI era: on Tao's blog, a case for valuing understanding over credit
stories.why_read: Yesterday's Calegari post was about practice. This one asks what mathematical work is for, once machines can produce proofs.
body: In a guest post on Terence Tao's blog, Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai and Jie Xue argue that AI forces mathematicians to ask what gives their work its worth. If the answer has become producing results and showing individual ability, they suggest, the current anxiety exposes a problem with that view of the work. Tao notes that the post itself was converted from another file format using AI.

They lean on a Platonic view: the primes were infinite before anyone proved it, so a mathematician's intelligence is a way to understand an order that exists independently. In that view, taste means recognizing which definitions and theorems reveal real structure, not a personal preference. The message for engineers is the same: don't measure yourself by output.

stories.headline: A 1995 Pentium Pro running modern Stockfish plays at about 3300 Elo. Deep Blue wasn't needed
stories.why_read: Nicholas Carlini shows that most of chess engines' progress since 1996 came from better algorithms, not faster hardware. You can play the machine live.
body: Deep Blue used 30 P2SC processors and 480 custom chess chips to search about 200 million positions per second. Carlini has a 200 MHz Pentium Pro with 64MB of RAM, released November 1, 1995, running a custom Stockfish port that plays at an estimated 3300 ± 87 Elo at classical time controls. Kasparov was rated just under 2800. The machine is online through a Realtek Ethernet card, so you can play it.

He also adds modern techniques one at a time to Crafty, a 1996 engine, including LMR, correction history, better quiescence search and NNUE evaluation. By his accounting, better programming explains about 720 of the 1,335 Elo points gained since then. It's a satisfying counterpoint to 'just add compute.'

stories.headline: Anthropic's IPO filing: 1,127% revenue growth, $107K a month per employee, and $895B in commitments
stories.why_read: The biggest IPO of the AI era is close, and the filing supports both the bull and bear cases.
body: Charlie Bilello's chart has Anthropic's Q3 revenue up 1,127% year over year, far ahead of SpaceX at 161% and Tesla at 0%. TechSpot, citing the amended S-1, reports $1.7 billion in Q3 personnel costs for about 5,300 people, roughly $107,300 per employee per month, $1.1 billion of it stock-based. Personnel was about 15% of the $33.2 billion in revenue for the first nine months of 2026.

On TechPolicy.Press, Matt Scherer argues the SEC should block the IPO. He cites about $895 billion in contractual commitments, including at least $582 billion that can't be canceled, owed to Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google and Microsoft, against $96 billion in cash. He also notes that the 2026 results are unaudited and argues that growth slowed over the summer. HN is split on whether he's right.

stories.headline: 97% of U.S. mortgage holders now pay less than today's rate, up from 54% in 2022
stories.why_read: One statistic that explains why the housing market is frozen.
body: Citing the Economist, @unusual_whales reports that 97% of U.S. homeowners with a mortgage now have a rate below the current market rate. In 2022, the figure was 54%.

That's the lock-in effect: almost nobody wants to give up a cheap mortgage for one above 7%, so inventory stays thin and prices stay high. It's a useful frame for any 'should we move' conversation in Austin.

stories.headline: On Election Day, new data shows the Republican gains among Indian Americans from 2024 have disappeared
stories.why_read: A sharp swing in the Indian American vote, especially among men 40 and older, in data released just ahead of today's midterms.
body: New survey data shared by @kharibiskut finds that Republican gains among Indian Americans in 2024 'seem to have disappeared,' and Republican support is the lowest the survey has recorded.

Milan Vaishnav's thread on the same data shows the sharpest shift among men 40 and older. Between January and October 2026, their Democratic support rose from 53% to 68%, while Republican support fell from 32% to 16%. Among Indian Americans overall, only Black Americans are more supportive of the Democratic Party.

stories.headline: Jared Isaacman defends the Lear 60 copilot whose last radio calls went viral
stories.why_read: A pilot with 8,000 hours asks people to stop speculating and show some decency to a crew who did their jobs until the end.
body: Writing in a personal capacity, Jared Isaacman, who has flown this class of aircraft for more than 20 years and logged over 8,000 hours, responds to commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from missile theories to DEI to critiques of the second-in-command's final radio calls. He says that last part troubles him most. She was doing her job, talking to ATC to the end in a terrifying situation, and likely knew she was going to die.

He points out that nobody outside the investigation knows the maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, or whether turbulence, overspeed or overcontrol played a part. He also notes that charter operators routinely pair early-career commercial pilots with ATP captains. It has passed 100,000 likes.

stories.headline: The world's problems began when the zebras with white stripes started disliking the zebras with black stripes
stories.why_read: A one-line reminder for Election Day that most divisions are about stripes on the same animal.
body: Prasanth Nair shared the line with a simple 'Have a lovely Monday,' and Anand bookmarked it.
It's a cartoon-sized joke about how arbitrary most of our tribal lines are. On a day when every feed will be loud, it's worth keeping in mind.

stories.headline: If you love a website, back it up
stories.why_read: A web archivist explains how easy it is to save your favorite corner of the web before it disappears.
body: The author works in web archiving and still lost a favorite site. Teapuppies.com, an Ochaken fan site online since 2004 and barely changed since 2005, disappeared, and its domain now serves online gambling ads. The point is that you don't have to wait for the Internet Archive. Saving a site is something you can do yourself.

The easiest option is the ArchiveWeb.page Chrome extension, which can save a single page, a whole site or a social profile in the standard WARC format. You can then replay it anywhere, even embedded in a blog post. The author discloses working for the company that makes the tools, and most of them are free.
